issues.legal_issue: A fatal shooting occurring during the same continuous attack as other shootings for which private defence was established may be treated as an exercise of that same right of private defence.
material_facts: The State appealed the High Court’s acquittal on the murder charge.

The trial court had found that the second deceased was killed while actively throwing stones and threatening the accused and his family, and had acquitted the accused on the basis of private defence; that acquittal was not appealed.
The evidence and physical traces of stones and broken bottles supported the account that a crowd was attacking the accused’s home.
The Supreme Court concluded that the shootings formed one incident and could not properly be divided into separate parts for purposes of assessing private defence.

The evidence also described a hostile confrontation between the accused and the first deceased on the previous evening, making the prosecution account that the deceased had been summoned and had arrived unsuspecting improbable.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was right to acquit the accused of the murder charge because the fatal shooting occurred as part of the same incident in which the accused was entitled to act in private defence. The State’s appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the right of private defence to the circumstances as a whole. Where multiple shootings form one continuous incident, and the circumstances establishing private defence for one shooting also apply to another, the incident should not be artificially divided to deny that defence. The charge was under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code. No earlier cases are cited in the supplied judgment.
